newsitem.title: INDIA: India mulls phasing out small engines to cut pollution.
newsitem.headline: India mulls phasing out small engines to cut pollution.

text.p: India is considering phasing out scooters and motorcycles with two-stroke engines in an effort to reduce air pollution in New Delhi, Environment Minister Saifuddin Soz said on Wednesday.
The government was also considering forcing two-wheelers and three-wheelers to use unleaded fuel in the capital, one of the world's most polluted cities, Soz told a news conference.

"We should consider the phasing out of two-stroke engines with four-stroke engines in two- and three-wheelers as two-stroke engines not only cause more pollution but are very fuel inefficient," Soz said.
"We have to see how pollution generated by two-wheelers can be controlled, by way of changing fuel, changing engines, getting back to manufacturers -- it is a big effort," he said.
Most of India's two-wheelers operate on two-stroke engines. Soz said about 2.6 million of the capital's 2.8 million vehicles were two- and three-wheelers.
Some three million scooters, mopeds and motorcycles were produced in Indian in the year ending March 31, 1996.
Motor vehicles generate about two-thirds of the 2,000 metric tonnes of air pollutants emitted every day in New Delhi, the world's fourth most polluted city.
In 1995, India made it mandatory for new cars to use unleaded fuel and ordered car makers to fit vehicles with catalytic converters to neutralise harmful emissions.

But most vehicles are old and do not have emission-control devices. Three-wheeled motorised scooter rickshaw drivers often top up their fuel tanks with kerosene, which is cheaper than petrol, and emits more toxic fumes.
Studies show about 7,500 people died prematurely in 1996 due to pollution-related diseases in New Delhi, and some 2.5 million people were treated for such illnesses.

Soz said the government planned to ban littering, finalise laws on disposal of bio-medical waste, and set up shared effluent treatment plants in industrial areas to prevent pollutants from flowing into the Yamuna River, the city's main source of water.
New Delhi generates more than 5,500 tonnes of solid waste daily, but only about 4,000 tonnes of garbage are collected and disposed of, the minister said.
